question.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+4x+13 & ={x}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+({2}^{2}-{2}^{2})+13 \\  & =({x}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2})-4+13 \\  & =(x+2)^{2}+9\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+4x+13}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x+2)^{2}+9}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+((x+2)/3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent:

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(\frac{x+2}{3}).$

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=\frac{x+2}{3}.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+4x+13}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+((x+2)/3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot 3\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x+2}{3})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
